chunks: What a cache is and how it works. The question: What is a cache?
A cache is a small, very fast memory between the processor and the slow main memory. It keeps copies of data the processor used recently, plus the data stored next to it.
The processor is far faster than main memory, so without a cache it would mostly wait. Programs reuse recent data and read neighbors, so a small cache answers most requests.
Think of the speed-dial list on a phone. It holds a few numbers, while the full phone book holds thousands.
Most calls go to people you called recently, so the short list usually has the number.
When it does not, you search the big book, add the number, and drop the one you used longest ago. The list is a copy of part of the book.
The index addresses one set, the tag is compared against every way in that set simultaneously, and the offset selects bytes within the matching 64-byte line.
The three field widths sum to the address width: 20 + 6 + 6 = 32.
Cache line: the chunk of memory, usually 64 bytes, that the cache copies in one go. Hit / miss: a hit finds the data in the cache.
A miss does not, so the line must come from main memory. Locality: programs tend to reuse recent data and read data next to it.
Tag: a label stored with each line, saying which memory address it copies. Eviction: throwing out an old line to make room for a new one.
A program adds up an array of 4-byte numbers in order. A 64-byte line holds 16 numbers. The first read misses, and the cache copies the whole line. The next 15 reads hit.
So the miss rate is 1 over 16 equals 6. 25 % . Say a hit takes 1 nanoseconds and each miss costs 80 nanoseconds extra. The average is 1 plus 0.
0625 times 80 equals 6 nanoseconds per read, instead of 80 nanoseconds with no cache. That is the whole idea.
"A cache is a small, fast SRAM between the CPU and main memory that holds copies of recently used data and instructions.
It works because of locality: programs reuse data and use neighboring data.

The address is split into tag, index and offset; the index selects a set, tags are compared, and a match is a hit in a cycle or few; otherwise it's a miss and a 64-byte line is fetched from the next level.
With a 95 percent hit rate and 80 nanoseconds DRAM, average access time falls from 80 nanoseconds to about 5 nanoseconds."
